Wikipedia recommender system: report¶

Information Retrieval project, Poznan University of Technology.

The system recommends English Wikipedia articles similar to a collection of visited ones. Input: a list of article titles or URLs. Output: a ranked list of corpus articles (title and link) with a score in [0, 1], and an explanation of each score.

Stage 1  crawler/        Vital articles lists ──► 2,200 articles ──► data/raw/articles_raw.parquet
Stage 2  preprocessing/  clean ► tokenize ► lemmatize + stem ──► data/processed/articles_processed.parquet
Stage 3  recommender/    TF-IDF + embeddings ► similarity ► interests ► top-k with scores
Stage 5  visualization/  corpus statistics and score breakdowns (this report)

Every chart below is computed from the data when the notebook runs; reports/figures/ keeps a copy of each. To try the recommender with your own articles, use notebooks/02_recommender_demo.ipynb or python -m wiki_recommender.recommender "Dog" "Cat".

Contents

  1. Crawling and scraping
  2. Preprocessing: stemming and lemmatization
  3. Scoring: how articles are recommended

def show(figure, name):
    """Display a chart and keep a copy in reports/figures."""
    figure = getattr(figure, "figure", figure)
    save(figure, name)
    plt.show()


def as_table(result) -> pd.DataFrame:
    return pd.DataFrame(
        [
            {
                "rank": r.rank,
                "title": r.title,
                "score": r.score,
                "text": r.signal_contributions["text"],
                "embedding": r.signal_contributions["embedding"],
                "compared with": ", ".join(r.interest),
                "shared terms": ", ".join(r.shared_terms[:4]),
            }
            for r in result.recommendations
        ]
    ).set_index("rank")

1. Crawling and scraping¶

Source. Articles come from English Wikipedia's Vital articles lists, levels 4 and 5, which sort about 50,000 important articles into 11 topics and thousands of subsections. Using them instead of a random walk over links gives a corpus that is broad, made of substantial articles, and labelled: each article carries its topic and subsection, which the evaluation later uses as ground truth.

Selection. Each topic gets the same quota of 200 articles:

  1. articles of levels 1-3 (such as World War II or Dog) are always taken;
  2. the rest is a 60/40 mix of level 4 articles and narrower level 5 ones, which add niche subjects;
  3. within a level, subsections take turns (round-robin), shuffled with a fixed seed so no subsection or alphabetical prefix can crowd out the others.

Filtering. Disambiguation pages, redirects to an article already collected, link collections (List of ..., Outline of ...), pages outside the main namespace and pages under 100 words are rejected.

Scraping. Each page is fetched with the MediaWiki action=parse API and its HTML is reduced to running prose: infoboxes, tables, navigation templates, figures, formulas, pronunciation guides, citation markers and trailing sections (See also, References, External links) are removed. The title, URL, lead section, section headings, categories and outgoing links are stored separately.

Politeness. A descriptive User-Agent, at least 0.25 s between requests, maxlag=5 (the crawler yields when Wikipedia's servers are busy) and exponential backoff on errors or Retry-After. An interrupted crawl resumes from a checkpoint.

2. Preprocessing: stemming and lemmatization¶

Cleaning. The crawler already removes most markup. This stage removes what is left: URLs, stray HTML tags, [[ ]] and {{ }} brackets, unfilled template parameters and repeated whitespace. Categories that describe Wikipedia's own maintenance (Articles with short description, Living people) are dropped, because they say nothing about the subject.

Tokens, lemmas and stems. Every article is tokenized once with spaCy (en_core_web_sm). Each word that passes one shared filter yields both a lemma (spaCy, part-of-speech aware) and a stem (NLTK Snowball), so the two token lists stay aligned word for word:

  • case and accents are folded (Müller = Muller);
  • stopwords, punctuation, numbers, ordinals (19th) and year ranges are removed; all-caps acronyms (US, WHO) are kept;
  • tokens must be Latin-script, 2 to 40 characters long and contain a letter (covid-19 survives).

Repairing lemmas. spaCy guesses the lemma of an unknown word by stripping a plural ending, which gives cryptocurrencie, or turns series into serie. After the whole corpus is read, such a guess is kept only if the corpus itself contains the singular at least a tenth as often as the plural: cryptocurrencies becomes cryptocurrency, while series and species stay whole. 4,413 lemmas were repaired this way.

Stored form. articles_processed.parquet keeps, for each article, the lemmas and the stems of its text, its definition (the first full lead paragraph, which says what the subject is), the length of its lead, and its lemmatized categories.

In [4]:
show(corpus.plot_vocabulary(stats), "vocabulary")
In [5]:
show(corpus.plot_top_words(stats, 25), "top_words")

Lemmas or stems? Stemming shrinks the vocabulary more, but it also merges unrelated words: universe and university share the stem univers, and united and unit share unit, which is why unit ranks far higher among stems than united among lemmas. Lemmas are real words, which keeps the term charts and score explanations readable (university, not univers).

The choice was also measured. Each representation is judged by how often an article's 10 nearest neighbours are related to it by signals that do not come from its text: the same Vital articles subsection, and a shared category from a held-out half of the categories. Settings were chosen on one half of the articles and measured on the other half (1,093 articles).

In [6]:
show(evaluation.plot_representation_eval(representation_eval), "representation_eval")
In [7]:
comparisons = pd.DataFrame(representation_eval["comparisons_on_test"]).T
comparisons.columns = ["difference", "95% low", "95% high"]
comparisons
Out[7]:
difference 95% low 95% high
final vs full text 0.030 2.139e-02 0.039
final vs definition only 0.099 8.545e-02 0.113
final vs lead only 0.049 3.588e-02 0.062
full text vs definition only 0.069 5.381e-02 0.086
final vs final, stemmed 0.004 -4.154e-04 0.008
full text vs full text, stemmed 0.007 3.432e-03 0.012

Lemmas beat stems by a small margin, but consistently (the paired bootstrap interval excludes zero), so lemmas are the canonical representation. Adding the definition again (weight 0.5) and the category tokens (weight 0.25) improves on the full text alone by +0.030. The final text vector of an article is

$$\mathbf{t} = \operatorname{norm}\big(\operatorname{norm}(\text{tfidf}(\text{article}) + 0.5\,\text{tfidf}(\text{definition})) \;\Vert\; 0.25\,\text{tfidf}(\text{categories})\big)$$

with sublinear TF ($1 + \log tf$), IDF fitted on the corpus, terms in at least two articles, and $\Vert$ the concatenation of the word and category features.

3. Scoring: how articles are recommended¶

3.1 Similarity of two articles¶

Two signals compare a visited article $v$ with a candidate $c$. Each is a cosine similarity in [0, 1]:

Signal Representation Weight
Text the TF-IDF vector $\mathbf{t}$ of section 2 0.55
Embedding BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 sentence embedding of the title and the first 150 words 0.45

$$s(v, c) = 0.55\,\cos_{\text{text}}(v, c) + 0.45\,\max\big(0, \cos_{\text{emb}}(v, c)\big)$$

The weights sum to 1, so $s(v, c) \in [0, 1]$. Text and embeddings complement each other: TF-IDF matches exact terms and names, the embedding matches meaning when the words differ.

3.2 From a history to one score¶

A history $V = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\}$ is first split into interests: visited articles are clustered with average linkage on $1 - s(v_i, v_j)$, and two stay together while their mean similarity is at least $t = 0.35$. For a candidate $c \notin V$ and an interest $I$:

$$\text{score}_I(c) = \frac{1}{|I|} \sum_{v \in I} s(v, c), \qquad \text{score}(c) = \max_I\, \text{score}_I(c)$$

The top-$k$ list is shared between interests in proportion to their size (each interest contributes its best candidates), visited articles are never recommended, and the list is sorted by score. With a single interest this is the plain mean, which ranks exactly like the centroid of the visited articles.

Why not just the mean? For a history about two unrelated subjects, the mean favours articles that sit between both and match neither well. Section 6 measures this.

3.3 Explaining a score¶

Because the score is a mean of weighted cosines, it splits exactly into parts. With $\mathbf{u}$ the mean text vector of the interest:

$$\text{score}(c) = \underbrace{\sum_{\text{terms } w} 0.55\, u_w\, c_w}_{\text{shared terms}} + 0.45\,\overline{\cos}_{\text{emb}} = \frac{1}{|I|}\sum_{v \in I} s(v, c)$$

The first form gives the waterfall charts (which shared words and which signals add up to the score), the second the per-visited-article charts (how much each visited article contributes).

Lengths are roughly log-normal: the median article has about 5,200 words, and the longest about 22,400. Preprocessing keeps about half of the words; most of the rest are stopwords. Biographies and history articles are the longest, mathematics articles the shortest.

4.2 Most important terms¶

The most frequent lemmas (section 2) are general words such as include, time and year. TF-IDF weights tell more: below, the highest mean weight over all articles (left), and for each topic the words that stand out most against the rest of the corpus.

In [11]:
show(corpus.plot_top_tfidf(model, 25), "top_tfidf")
In [12]:
show(corpus.plot_topic_terms(model, 8), "topic_terms")

Each topic is recognisable from its words alone. Two artefacts of lemmatization show here: in People, bear is the lemma of born, and in Geography mi and sq come from sq mi, the area unit.

4.3 Similarities between documents¶

Similarities among 2,000 random articles (about 2 million pairs), for each signal and for the combined score $s$:

In [13]:
sample = corpus.similarity_sample(model, size=2000)
show(corpus.plot_similarity_distributions(sample), "similarity_distributions")

The two signals behave very differently. Text vectors are sparse, so most pairs of unrelated articles share almost nothing. Embeddings are never far apart: even unrelated articles have a cosine of about 0.5. The combined score therefore has a floor of about 0.2 for unrelated articles, and good recommendations score roughly 0.4-0.6.

In [14]:
show(corpus.plot_same_vs_other_topic(sample), "same_vs_other_topic")
In [15]:
topics = corpus.topic_similarity_matrix(sample)
show(corpus.plot_topic_heatmap(topics), "topic_similarity")

Articles are most similar within their own topic (the diagonal). Mathematics is the most self-contained topic. The strongest pair of different topics is Geography and History, followed by Mathematics and Physical sciences: countries and empires, and the mathematics of physics.

In [16]:
show(corpus.plot_nearest_neighbour(model, sample), "nearest_neighbour")

For almost every article the corpus holds a clearly related one, scoring well above the 0.2 floor of unrelated pairs: the corpus is dense enough to recommend from.

4.4 A map of the corpus¶

A 2D t-SNE map of the embeddings of the 2,200 articles. Eleven topics are too many to tell apart by color in one picture, so each panel highlights one topic over the whole map.

In [17]:
points = corpus.embedding_map(model, size=3000)
show(corpus.plot_embedding_map(points), "embedding_map")

Biology, Mathematics, Geography and Philosophy and religion form compact regions. People, History, Society and Technology are spread out, because they touch every other subject: a biography of a physicist sits next to physics, not next to other biographies.

All three visited articles form one interest, so every score is their mean similarity, and each contributes about a third (right chart). The recommendations are the neighbouring genres. The waterfall shows which shared words matter: genre, blue (the lemma of blues), jazz, music, rock and roll. Most of the text part is spread over many smaller shared terms, and the embedding adds the largest share.

5.4 An article outside the corpus¶

Information retrieval is not among the 2,200 articles. It is fetched from Wikipedia, extracted and preprocessed exactly like the corpus (Stages 1 and 2), vectorized with the fitted model, and then used like any visited article. Without internet access it is reported as unresolved instead.

In [24]:
unseen = recommender.recommend(["Information retrieval", "Search engine"], top_k=8)
print(unseen)
if unseen.recommendations:
    show(breakdown.explain(unseen, rank=1), "example_unseen_top")

5.5 Inputs that cannot be used¶

Misspelled titles, disambiguation pages and URLs that are not Wikipedia articles are reported with the reason and close titles; the remaining inputs are still used.

6. Evaluation and limitations¶

The signals, their weights and the aggregation were chosen with the same offline protocol as the text representation (section 2): an article's recommendations count as related if they share its Vital articles subsection or a held-out category. Settings were tuned on half of the articles and are reported on the other half.

6.1 Signals¶

In [26]:
show(evaluation.plot_signal_eval(recommender_eval), "signal_eval")
In [27]:
signals = pd.DataFrame(recommender_eval["single_article_comparisons_on_test"]).T
signals.columns = ["difference", "95% low", "95% high"]
signals
Out[27]:
difference 95% low 95% high
text + bge-small, 1 passage vs text 0.015 0.009 0.022
text + bge-small, 1 passage vs bge-small, 1 passage 0.026 0.018 0.034

Text and embeddings together beat text alone by +0.015 and the embedding alone by +0.026. bge-small beat MiniLM-L6, and embedding more than the first passage did not help once combined with text.

6.2 Aggregating a history¶

Simulated histories: one interest (3 or 5 articles of one subsection) or two interests (3 + 2 articles from subsections of different topics). Coverage is the share of interests that get at least one recommendation.

In [28]:
show(evaluation.plot_aggregation_eval(recommender_eval), "aggregation_eval")
In [29]:
show(evaluation.plot_interest_threshold(recommender_eval), "interest_threshold")

Splitting a history into interests costs almost nothing when it has one topic (−0.001) and gains +0.102 over the mean when it has two; it also serves 91 % of the interests instead of 69 %. A threshold of 0.35 is the best trade-off: lower values merge unrelated interests, higher values split one interest apart.

6.3 Limitations¶

  • Scores are relative. Because embeddings never drop far below 0.5, unrelated articles still score about 0.2. A score is meaningful compared with other scores, not as an absolute probability.
  • The corpus bounds the answers. Recommendations come only from the 2,200 articles; an article fetched on the fly can be visited, but is never recommended.
  • Relevance is approximated. Subsections and categories are a proxy for what a reader finds related; they do not reward surprising but useful recommendations.
  • No diversity re-ranking. Within one interest, near-duplicates (e.g. Roman Republic and Roman Empire) can both appear.
